book.title: Ebba Thorn's Reckoning
book.author: Ebba Thorn
pages:
What is owed me, and what I am owed. E.T. her hand.

The tanner's girl, for the pains: two of feverfew, one of willow. Paid in eggs.

The drover, for his dog: nothing to be done. Paid anyway. A good man.

The hill house: one measure of the grey. To be taken in milk, a pinch at the new moon. Paid in silver thread, by the hand that always pays.

The hill house: second measure. The hand asked how long. I said: done slow, a season. Done quick, the healer will know it, and then the watch will know it.

The miller, for his wife's trouble. Ask no more of that.

My sister says I will hang for the hill house. My sister has never once paid for her own bread.

The hill house: third measure. The hand shook. I said it is not too late. A man comes back from two measures. A man comes back from three, if he is fed on honey and kept warm and his cup is watched. From four, nobody comes back.

The hand paid for four.

The fourth to be fetched at the dark of the moon, from the stump at the crossways, as before.

Somebody has been at my door in the night. Not the watch. The watch knocks.

I have put the fourth measure in the stump at the crossways. Whoever comes for it, I want no more of the hill house. Let it be on the hand that pays.

If my sister reads this: the grey is in the blue jar. The answer to it is in the brown, and there is not much of it.

hut.name: Ebba Thorn's hut in the fen

carr.name: the alder carr behind the hut

to_stump.journal: A ledger came off a dead witch. Ebba Thorn sold a slow poison she called the grey, a measure at a time, to somebody of a hill house. Three measures had been taken. A man comes back from three. Nobody comes back from four, and the fourth was left in a stump at the crossways.

search_stump.goal: Search the stump at the crossways

clues.name: A twist of grey powder
lore: Wrapped in a dock leaf, small as a thumb.
It smells of nothing at all. A pinch in milk at the new moon, the ledger says.
clues.journal: The fourth measure was still in the stump. Nobody had come for it.

clues.name: Silver thread
lore: The twist is tied with silver thread, fine as hair, the kind braid is worked with.
Paid in silver thread, by the hand that always pays.
clues.journal: The twist was tied with silver braiding thread, the stuff the hand had paid in.

clues.name: A small glove
lore: A woman's glove, lined, trodden into the mud behind the stump.
The fingertips are stained grey, as if with ash or with something finer.
clues.journal: A woman's glove lay trodden in the mud behind the stump, grey at the fingertips.

clues.name: A round tag
lore: A little iron tag with a number punched through it.
The watch hang these at the belt to count their night rounds. This one's cord is snapped.
clues.journal: A watchman's round tag lay at the foot of the stump, its cord snapped.

clues.name: A chalk mark
lore: Drawn on the bark at the height a child draws: a house on a hill, and beside it a moon.
Under them, four strokes. Three are crossed through.
clues.journal: A child had chalked a house on a hill and a moon on the stump, and four strokes, three crossed through.

healer.goal: Speak with whoever tends the sick at {place:house}
say: Boots off at the door, and quiet. He sleeps badly and wakes worse. I am {healer}. I keep the Hearthkeeper's hearth in this town, and I have kept {elder} alive since harvest on honey and stubbornness.

A wasting nobody can name. Grey at the lips, cold in the hands, a little worse every new moon and a little better between. I have prayed over him and bled him and fed him, and I am out of things to do. Why are you looking at me like that?

replies.say: Read this. The hill house is in a witch's ledger.
Who in this house pays in silver thread?

say: The grey. She calls it the grey. Hearthkeeper keep us, I have been fighting a fever that was a hand all along. A pinch at the new moon, and the new moon is in four days.

Silver thread? Everybody in this house. {elder} made his name in braid. His wife, {wife}, works it still, and his son, {son}, sells it at market when he is not on the watch. It is the coin of this house.
If the answer is in that brown jar, I want it. A man comes back from three, she says. I want him back. Bring me the jar, and I will watch his cup myself, and I will not sleep.

replies.say: I'll fetch the brown jar.
replies.journal: {healer}, who keeps the Hearthkeeper's hearth, had nursed {elder} of the hill house since harvest. His wife, {wife}, and his son, {son}, of the watch, both dealt in silver thread. The new moon was four days off.

replies.say: Burn the ledger. I'll not hang a house on a witch's word.
replies.journal: The witch's ledger went into the hill house fire.

?hand=wife: The healer says you are going into the fen for him. That is kind. That is very kind of you.
Will he live, do you think? No. Do not answer. I will fetch the honey for his milk. I always fetch it. Excuse me. My arm is stiff today, I slept on it.
?hand=elder: The healer says you are going into the fen for him. Do you know, he will not have her near him at the new moon any more. He asks for his milk himself. He holds the cup himself, with both hands, as if somebody would take it.
Go if you must. I will keep the house. I have kept it since harvest.
?: The healer says you are going into the fen for him. Bless you. I have sat up with him every night since harvest and I am so tired I cannot see the braid.

Hal has been good. Hal sits with him when the watch lets him. He is out at nights a great deal, the watch works him hard, and he is short of money, and I do not ask. A grown son does not want his father's wife asking.

replies.say: Who brings him his milk?
I'll be back before the new moon.

?hand=son: You are the one with a book. The healer told me. Give it to me and I will take it to the watch myself, it is my watch, it will be quicker.
No? Well. As you like. What else did the healer say? Did she say how long?
?hand=elder: You are the one with a book. The healer told me. I am the watch, and I have seen nothing in this house but a sick old man.
Though he did pay the tanner's boy a coin a month back, to run to the crossways with a message. A wager, he said. My father has never made a wager in his life.
?: You are the one with a book. The healer told me. I am the watch, and I would like to see it, when you are done.
He is a hard man, my father. He has been hard on her. I have told him so, and he laughed at me, and that was that. Do not judge this house by her face. Judge it by his hand.

journal.?hand=son: {son} of the watch asked for the witch's ledger, to take it to the watch himself, and asked how long his father had.
journal.?hand=elder: {son} said his father paid the tanner's boy to run a message to the crossways a month back, and called it a wager.
journal.?: {wife} seemed afraid, and kept her arm still. {son} said his father had been hard on her.

sister.goal: Speak with whoever keeps the hut
say: Stop there. I know that book. I bound it for her. I know whose hands it came out of, too, because she is not in the hut, and she was never once away a night.
You killed my sister on the road, and now you have come to her shelves. Say why, and say it quickly. I have been shouting her name at the fen since the crows came.

replies.say: She came at me with fire and a blade.
There's a man in a hill house with three measures of her grey in him.

say: She came at you. Yes. She would have. She had been jumping at shadows for a month: somebody at the door at night, she said. Not the watch. The watch knocks.

The hill house. She wanted done with it. She said it every night: let it be on the hand that pays. The brown jar is on her shelf. It is the last of it, and it was mine as much as hers, and you owe me a sister.
sister_more.journal: Ebba Thorn's sister, {sister}, kept the hut in the fen. Ebba had been afraid for a month of somebody at her door at night.

replies.say: Then let me pay for her burying. {coins:15}.
replies.journal: {coins:15} went to {sister} for her sister's burying.

returns.say: I buried her by the alder with your coin, and then I sat in the hut and thought. Somebody at the door at night, she said. I found where they stood. Silver thread caught on the bramble by the window, and the print of town boots. The hand that pays wanted to be sure she would never tell. She is dead, so they have their wish. Watch that house.

replies.say: I am sorry for her. I would not have had it so.
replies.journal: {sister} was told it was not wished. She let the jar go for the sick man's sake.

returns.say: Sorry. You were sorry. I said I would let the jar go for the old man's sake, and I did. I never said I would let you go. She was all I had.

replies.say: Stand aside, or lie down with her.
What would you take, to call it quits between us?

say: Not coin. Coin is what she took, and look where it put her.

Somebody stood at her window at night for a month and frightened her out onto the road, and the road had you on it. That was the hand that pays. I want the name of that hand before the watch has it and before the hill house has it. Bring it to me first.

Do that, and the brown jar is yours with no blood and no burying money. Her test is on the shelf with it, if the house wants showing after. She never sold a measure without it: a buyer who swore a twist was not opened had to wet their fingers first. What it asks for grows in the carr behind this hut and shows only by night. But the name comes here before any bowl is filled. There is one measure left in the blue jar. A measure for a measure. That is my bargain.

voices.law: A name carried to a witch's sister before the watch hears it is no kind of justice. Think what she means to do with it.
voices.vengeance: She has the right of it. Somebody drove her sister onto that road. Let her have the name.

replies.say: You'll have the name before anybody.
replies.journal: {sister} let the brown jar go on a bargain: the name of the hand that pays, brought to her before the watch or the hill house have it. She means to see it paid, a measure for a measure.

replies.say: The jar, for the sick man's sake. But the name goes where it is owed, and that is not the fen.

try.refuse: Then we have no bargain, and you are back to coin or steel. Choose.

replies.journal: {sister} let the brown jar go for the sick man's sake, and was promised nothing for it.

replies.say: No bargain. Here is {coins:15} for her burying, and that is all.
replies.journal: {coins:15} went to {sister} for her sister's burying.

returns.say: I buried her by the alder with your coin, and then I sat in the hut and thought. Somebody at the door at night, she said. I found where they stood. Silver thread caught on the bramble by the window, and the print of town boots. The hand that pays wanted to be sure she would never tell. She is dead, so they have their wish. Watch that house.

replies.say: No bargain. Stand aside.

fight_sister.taunt: Then come and finish what you started on the road.
fight_sister.plea: Stop. Stop, I yield. I'll not be the last of us lying in the fen over a jar of honey.
fight_sister.mercy: Then live, and stay out of my way.
fight_sister.thanks: Take the jar. I will remember that you could have, and did not.

spared_returns.say: There is nobody in the fen now but me and the crows, and the crows are poor company. I know every root and leaf between here and the hills, which will heal and which will kill. You let me up off the mud when you had no reason to. I would like to walk with somebody who does that.

search_hut.goal: Search Ebba Thorn's shelves for the brown jar

clues.name: The brown jar
lore: Brown clay, stoppered with wax. A finger's depth of something thick and bitter-sweet.
Scratched in the wax with a pin: the answer.
clues.journal: The brown jar was on Ebba's shelf. There was not much in it.

clues.name: The blue jar
lore: Blue glaze, nearly empty. A fine grey dust in the bottom.
Enough for one more measure. No more than that.
clues.journal: The blue jar held enough of the grey for one more measure.

clues.name: A receipt in Ebba's hand
lore: 'The tell. Galls off the fen alder, cut by night, when the ripe ones show pale. Steep them a day in strong spirit.'
'A hand that has opened the grey goes black to the wrist in it and stays black a week. Wet every buyer's fingers. Take nobody's word.'
clues.journal: Ebba kept a receipt for a test she called the tell: galls cut by night from the fen alders and steeped in strong spirit. A hand that has touched the grey goes black in it.

clues.name: A letter in a careful hand
lore: 'You said there is a way that looks like a fever. I have three children and he has broken my arm twice. Name your price. M.'
Folded small and kept, as if Ebba wanted something to show if it came to it.
clues.journal: Ebba had kept a letter signed M.: a woman with three children whose husband had broken her arm twice, asking for a way that looks like a fever.

clues.name: A note of hand
lore: 'Four measures, paid on the fourth. The house sells by spring or the dice men have my hands. H.'
Kept under a jar, with the thread still tied round it.
clues.journal: Ebba had kept a note signed H.: the house must sell by spring, or the dice men would have his hands.

clues.name: A letter in a shaking hand
lore: 'Make it slow, and make it look like the wasting. If I die of my own hand they will bury me outside the wall, and my wife gets nothing. The thread is from my own loom. A.'
The letters climb the page like a man writing in bed.
clues.journal: Ebba had kept a letter signed A.: a man who wanted to die slowly, of something that looked like a wasting, so that his wife would keep the house.

bring_jar.goal: Bring the brown jar to {healer} before the new moon

give.name: Ebba's brown jar
lore: Thick, bitter-sweet, and not much of it.
The answer to the grey.

bring_jar.journal: The brown jar reached {healer} at the hill house before the new moon.

lines: He has had the answer, all of it, in warm milk and honey from my own hand, and nobody else has been near his cup. The new moon came and went, and last night he sat up and asked for bread.
Then he asked who had done it. I did not tell him, because I do not know, and I would not guess in this house.
{wife} has not slept. {son} has been in and out with the watch and will not sit down. {elder} has asked for you. Come to the hill house.

?hand=elder: You. You went into the fen and brought back the brown jar. Do you know what you have done? I was nearly through. Three measures, and the pain going grey and far off, like the sea at night.

I paid for four. My wife has three children and no trade of her own but the braid. If I die by my own hand the Truth's men bury me outside the wall, and the house goes to my brother. If I die of a wasting, she keeps it. Do you see? Do you see what you have done?
?: So you are the one who went into the fen for me. Sit. I am told I was poisoned. I am told it like a weather report. I have had three wives and buried two, and I know what this house thinks of me.
Find me the hand. I will not have it said I died of my own cup in my own house, and I will not have the one who did it eating my bread.

replies.say: There is a fourth measure. If you want it, it is yours.
replies.journal: The fourth measure went back to {elder}, at his own asking.

replies.say: Let me speak with your household first.
The witch kept a test for the grey. Give me two nights, and the whole house will see whose hand it was.
replies.journal: I told {elder} of Ebba's test for the grey, and asked two nights to make it.

replies.say: I have nothing to tell this house yet. The name is owed in the fen first.
replies.journal: I kept my bargain with {sister}. The name went to the fen before the watch or the house heard it from me.

gather.goal: Gather alder galls in {place:carr} by night

clues.name: Pale alder galls
lore: Hard little apples on the alder twigs. By day they are bark brown, and nobody would pick them out.
By night the ripe ones show pale, like teeth. These are the ones she cut.
clues.journal: By night the ripe galls on the fen alders showed pale as teeth. I cut a pocketful.

clues.name: A gall knife on a cord
lore: A hooked knife hung in the fork of the oldest alder, its cord gone green.
The handle is worn to the shape of one hand. She came here on a great many nights.
clues.journal: Ebba's gall knife still hung in the oldest alder, the handle worn to her hand.

clues.name: Last year's galls
lore: Under the tree lie the galls nobody cut, gone black and soft.
Crushed between finger and thumb, one leaves a stain that will not rub off. It is the black that clerks make their ink from.
clues.journal: The galls nobody cut lay black under the tree. Crushed, they stain like ink.

brew.goal: Distil strong spirits at a still, and bring them to {healer} with the galls

give.name: A pocketful of pale galls
lore: Cut by night in the carr behind Ebba Thorn's hut.
To be steeped a day in strong spirit.

brew.journal: I fermented a cask and ran it through a still, and took the spirit and the galls to {healer}. She set them steeping in a bowl on the hearth and let nobody near it.

?hand=wife: It has gone the colour of sloes. I had the whole house in, and {elder} carried down in his chair. One at a time, I said, to the wrist, and hold it there while I count ten.

The children first, to show them it was only cold. Then {son}. Clean. Then her. She put her right hand in without being asked twice, and it came out black to the wrist, and she stood holding it out in front of her as if it were somebody else's.
Nobody spoke. The old man looked at that hand a long time. Then he looked at her other arm, the one that set crooked. She is in the braid room. Go gently, or do not go.
?hand=son: It has gone the colour of sloes. I had the whole house in, and {elder} carried down in his chair. One at a time, I said, to the wrist, and hold it there while I count ten.
Her first. Clean. The children, clean. Then {son} said the watch does not put its hands in a witch's bowl, and his father said from the chair: put it in. It came out black to the wrist.
He said the bowl was dirty. I washed it in front of him and filled it again. He would not put the other hand in. He is on the stair. He has his sword on.
?: It has gone the colour of sloes. I had the whole house in, and {elder} carried down in his chair. One at a time, I said, to the wrist, and hold it there while I count ten.
Her, clean. {son}, clean. I was reaching for the cloth when the old man said: and mine. I told him there was no need. He said it again.

Black to the knuckle, both hands. He held them up to the room like a man showing what he has caught. His wife did not look surprised. I shall be a long time thinking about that. She is in the braid room.

journal.?hand=wife: The test was made before the whole hill house. {wife}'s right hand came out of the bowl black to the wrist.
journal.?hand=son: The test was made before the whole hill house. {son}'s hand came out of the bowl black to the wrist, and he would not put the other in.
journal.?: The test was made before the whole hill house. {elder} asked to put his own hands in. They came out black to the knuckle.

replies.say: I'll go in and speak.
The whole house saw the bowl. Let the house judge its own. Not the watch, and not me.
replies.journal: I left it to the hill house to judge its own, since the whole house had seen the hand come out of the bowl.

?hand=wife: You found my letter. I knew she kept things. Everybody said she kept things.

Look at my arm. Look how it set. Twice. And the boy's ear, that does not hear now. I went to the watch once, and the watch is his son. So I went into the fen. I went three times. I could not go a fourth. That is why it is still in the stump. I could not.
?hand=son: Shut the door. You have the look of somebody holding a paper.

I owe the dice men more than this house is worth, and he will not sell. He would sooner leave it to the Truth's house than see me spend it. Do you know what they do to a watchman's hands? I made it slow. I would have sat with him to the end. I did sit with him. There is {coins:20} in the market chest. Take it, and let it have been a fever.
?: You have been talking to him. Shut the door, then.

I know. I have known since the second new moon. He paid in thread from his own loom, and I keep the count of every hank in this house. I said nothing. I watched him get better between and worse at the dark and I said nothing, because he asked me with his eyes not to. Now he is mending, and he hates you, and I do not know what I feel.

replies.say: The watch will hear of this.
Take the children and go tonight. I'll say it was a fever.
replies.journal: {wife} was let go in the night with her children, and the house was told it was a fever.

returns.say: We are two valleys over, with my cousin, and the boy laughs now. He never laughed in that house. I do not know what you are owed for it. I only know nobody else in the whole town lifted a hand. I worked this on the road. It is the only thing I know how to make.

replies.say: You'll go before the ruler for this.
{coins:20}, and it was a fever.
replies.journal: {son} paid {coins:20} from the market chest, and it was called a fever.

replies.say: Say it to him yourself, at his bedside.

journal.?hand=son: {son} was told to go to his father's bedside and say it.
journal.?: {wife} was told to go to {elder}'s bedside and say it.

foe_son.taunt: Then I am dead either way, and I would sooner it was a blade than a rope.
foe_son.plea: Stop! I yield. I am his son. Whatever I did, I am still his son.
foe_son.mercy: Then go up and say it to him.
foe_son.thanks: I'll say it. Hearthkeeper help me, I'll say it.

spared_returns.say: He put me out of the house the same night. The watch took my tag. The dice men took the rest. Everything I had, gone in one evening on a stair, because you would not take twenty and walk away. Well. I have friends who also have nothing left to lose.

son_yields.say: I'll go up. I'll say it. Do not come with me. Let me at least do that much on my own feet.
son_yields.journal: {son} went up the stair alone to say it to his father himself.

?mark:fm_judged: The watch came for {wife} the next morning. It was not {son} who came; he would not. {elder} sat up in bed to watch her taken, and asked for his breakfast after.
The ruler gave her the rope. The children are his to raise now. The eldest has stopped speaking. I bring honey to the house every day, and nobody eats it.
?mark:fm_fled: {wife} is gone, and the children with her, in the night, with a cart and the good blankets. {elder} raged until he coughed blood, and then he stopped.
I told the house it was a fever, a long one, and it broke. I have never said a thing in the Hearthkeeper's name that I knew to be false until now. I said it, and I would say it again.
?mark:fm_bought: {elder} mends. He walks to the gate and back now. {son} brings him his milk every evening, and sits with him while he drinks it, and holds his hand.
I watch the cup. I will always watch the cup. I do not know why I feel it is my own cup I am watching.
?mark:fm_eased: {elder} died at the new moon, in his sleep, with his wife's hand in his. I named it a wasting. The Truth's men gave him the rite and buried him inside the wall, and the house is hers.
She said you had given him something. I did not ask what. I have kept this hearth twenty years, and I have learned there are some things the Hearthkeeper remembers and some she lets go.
?mark:fm_son_spared: {son} went up the stair and said it to his father, all of it, the dice and the grey. {elder} listened to the end. Then he put his son out of the house in his shirt, and called for the watch to take his tag.
He lives, {elder}. He is stronger every day. He says he will see the house go to the Truth's house before his son has a thread of it.
?hand=wife: {wife} went up to him and said it, the arm, the boy's ear, the fen. I was outside the door. He did not shout. He was quiet so long I went in.
He had his face to the wall. She is still in the house. I do not know what was agreed between them. He has not raised his hand since. I do not know if it will last.
?: {wife} went up and told him she had known since the second new moon, and said nothing. He wept. I have never seen him weep.

He lives. He sits in the sun by the door, and she sits by him with the braid, and nobody in the house speaks of the fen. He is angry with you still. I think that will pass. I think he did not know she would rather have him.

lines: {elder} heard it from his bed: the blades on the stair and the fall. He made me help him down to see. He sat on the bottom step beside his son a long while.
The watch has called it what it was. There were dice men at the burying, at the back, who wanted to know who would pay what {son} owed. {elder} paid them. He lives. I do not think he is glad of it.

?hand=wife: The house sat on it two days with the door shut, {elder} in his chair, and {son} with his tag off and laid on the table, so that he sat as a son and not as the watch.

They have judged it between them. She goes to her cousin two valleys over with the children, and has a third of the braid money every quarter day for as long as she keeps away. He keeps the house. {son} carried her boxes down himself. Nobody said the word rope.
The old man asked to see her arm before she went. She showed him. He did not say he was sorry. He said: a third, every quarter day. I think it is the nearest he can come.
?hand=son: The house sat on it two days with the door shut. {son} laid his tag on the table before anybody asked him to.

His father has paid the dice men every coin, in front of witnesses, and bound him to the loom for seven years to work it off. No watch, no market, no dice, and his bed in the braid loft. {wife} holds the paper. It was her notion. She said a rope pays nobody back.
He still brings the old man his milk. {elder} makes him drink from the cup first. They both seem to find that fair.
?: There was nothing to judge in the end, only something to be said aloud. He said it: that he paid for his own death so that she should keep the house, and that he would do it again.

{wife} had the town book fetched up the hill, and stood beside her black-handed husband while it was written in that the house is hers, whatever he dies of and wherever they bury him. It cost her the good loom to have it written.
He has stopped asking after the blue jar. He sits in the sun. His hands are black yet, and he will not wear gloves.

to_sister.goal: Take the name to {sister} in the fen

sister_name.journal: {sister} took the name. She said we were quits.

?hand=wife: The wife. So it was the one with the arm. Ebba said the hand shook.

I'll not send the grey after a woman with three children at her skirts. I am not my sister, and my sister would not have done it either. But she will find a twist tied with fen grass on her sill at the new moon, with nothing in it but ash. Let her open it, and think about windows.
Go on. We are quits, you and I. I did not think I would ever say that to you.
?hand=son: The watchman. Town boots at her window. I knew they were town boots.

He frightened her out onto that road to save himself a debt. Then he has a debt in the fen as well, and the fen does not take a note of hand. There is one measure in the blue jar. He likes his dice. Let him wonder which cup.
Go on. We are quits, you and I. I did not think I would ever say that to you.
?: Himself. He paid her to kill him slowly, and then somebody of his stood at her window to see that she kept her mouth shut.

Then there is nobody to pay. He has had three of his four already, and thanked her for each. I'll not waste the blue jar on a man who wants it. But I will stand at his gate at the new moon and tell him he still owes for the fourth, and that I shall be at his burying to collect, whenever it is.
Go on. We are quits, you and I. I did not think I would ever say that to you.

?hand=wife: At the new moon there was a twist tied with fen grass on {wife}'s sill. She cried out so that I heard it from the hearth. There was nothing in it but ash.

She has told him everything since: the arm, the fen, the three measures. I think she believed the fourth had come for her. He has not raised his hand. The watch has not been told, and I am not going to be the one who tells it.
?hand=son: {son} took sick at the new moon. Grey at the lips and cold in the hands. I know that sickness now, and so does he.

He has told his father all of it from his bed: the dice, the stump, the window in the fen. There is no more of the answer. You brought me the last, and it went into the old man. I am feeding the son honey and watching his cup. A man comes back from two, she wrote, and he has had one. I mean to hold her to that.
?: A woman from the fen stood at the hill house gate at the new moon and would not come in. She said one thing to {elder} through the bars, and went.

He has not asked after the blue jar since. He asked me whether a man can owe the dead. I told him what the Hearthkeeper remembers is what the living keep tending. He is mending, and tending something. I told his wife the whole of it. Somebody had to.

burned.text: Ebba Thorn's ledger went into the hill house fire, and nobody went into the fen for the brown jar.

judged.text: {wife} was named to the watch and hanged for the grey in her husband's milk. {elder} lives, and their children are his to raise.
town: They hanged the braid-woman from the hill house. Poisoner, they say. Her poor husband.
Did you see her arm? Nobody looked at her arm.

lines: I let the jar go on your word. The name first, you said, before the watch and before the house. I have it now from a drover, third hand, like everybody else in this country.

I do not send the grey after oath-breakers. I only tell them what they are. You took a dead woman's shelf on a promise and did not keep it. The fen is shut to you. Do not come gathering here by night again.

fled.text: {wife} took her children and went in the night. {elder} lives, and the house was told it was a fever.
town: The old braid-master's wife ran off with the children and the good blankets. After all he gave her.
A fever, the healer says. Long one. Broke, in the end.

bought.text: {son} paid {coins:20} for it to have been a fever. {elder} mends, and his son brings him his milk every evening.
town: The old braid-master's on his feet again. That son of his never leaves his side. Good lad.
The healer's taken to calling at the hill house at milk-time. Every evening. Odd, that.

text.?mark:fm_son_spared: {son} said it to his father himself. {elder} lives, and put his son out of the house in his shirt.
text.?hand=wife: {wife} said it to {elder} herself, all of it. He lives, and she is still in the house, and he has not raised his hand since.
text.?: {elder} lives, and knows his wife saw the grey and said nothing because he asked her with his eyes. She sits by him in the sun.

town: Something happened up at the hill house. They're all very quiet up there now.
The braid-master's sitting out by his door in the sun. Never once saw him do that before.

returns.say: I came to say the hill house is still standing, and everybody in it. I did not think it would be. I have kept the Hearthkeeper's hearth twenty years, and I have learned that most of what I do is watch a cup. You went into the fen instead. Take these, and keep them by you.

son_slain.text: {son} drew on the hill house stair and died of it. {elder} lives, and paid his son's debts to the dice men at the burying.
town: The braid-master's son, killed on his own father's stair. Watchman, too.
Dice men at a burying. Bold as you like. The old man paid them, they say.

eased.text: {elder} had his fourth measure at the new moon. He was buried inside the wall as a man who died of a wasting, and his wife keeps the house.
town: Old braid-master's gone. Wasting, the healer says. Peaceful, at the end.
His widow's kept the house and the loom. Good. She works harder than he ever did.

returns.say: He went easy. He was holding my hand and he said the sea was a long way off now. I do not know what you gave him and I am not going to ask. The house is mine and the children's. This is the last braid he worked. He would want you to have it, I think. I would.

text.?hand=wife: The test showed {wife}'s hand before the whole hill house, and the house judged its own. She went to her cousin's with the children and a third of the braid money. {elder} lives. Nobody said the word rope.
text.?hand=son: The test showed {son}'s hand before the whole hill house, and the house judged its own. His father paid the dice men and bound him seven years to the loom. {elder} lives, and his son drinks from his cup first.
text.?: The test showed {elder}'s own hands before the whole hill house. He said aloud what he had paid for, and his wife had it written in the town book that the house is hers whatever he dies of. He lives.

town: They had the witch's bowl out at the hill house, and every hand in it. I'd not have put mine in, and I have nothing to hide.
The braid-master's house settled its own trouble with the door shut. The watch was never sent for. Make of that what you like.

text.?hand=wife: I took the name to the fen, as I had bargained. {sister} sent {wife} a twist of ash and nothing worse. The hill house knows the whole of it now, and the watch was never told.
text.?hand=son: I took the name to the fen, as I had bargained. {son} took a measure of the grey at the new moon, and may yet come back from it. {elder} lives, and knows what his son did.
text.?: I took the name to the fen, as I had bargained. {sister} would not spend the last of the grey on a man who wanted it. {elder} lives, and has been told what he owes.

town: There was a fen woman at the hill house gate at the new moon. Stood there like a post. Nobody asked her in.
Something came to the hill house off the fen, and it was not a fever. They are all very careful with their cups up there.

returns.say: I poured the last of the blue jar into the bog and broke the jar after it. Ebba's trade ends with Ebba. I keep bees now. The fen is good for them, and nobody is afraid of honey. You kept your word to me when the watch and the house would both have paid you better. This is the first of it.
